items.title: Ernest "Punch" Miller Interview, 1957-multiple
items.q: Well, I was in the Army and I used to go on watching him. I had my music up there but I'm watching his fingers, see? Every time he'd touch a bass I'd touch one. So he said, uh-uh, you can't make it like that. He said, you better learn some music. So he started to show him.

ctx.x: I could just whistle something up and pick the horn up and blow it. I don't know what key I was on unless I knew I played. And, uh, who taught you how to read it? Well, I liked something in the Army. I stole my reading. That's the truth I stole. A fella named Chip used to be there. Yeah, he did. Now, you heard of him. His name was Lewis Mathis. He was one of his kid over at trumpet players way back years ago and called him Chip. Well, I was in the Army and I used to go on watching him. I had my music up there but…
He's daddy, huh? Which, no, which Willie Humphrey? I mean there's a- The old man. Not Willie Humphrey would play the clarinet.

items.title: Ernest 'Punch' Miller Interview, 1960-04-04
items.q: Chip used to sit right side me and show me a lot of notes see.

ctx.x: Well when you started off with a teacher did the teacher make you practice much? Well guess how that

happened. I didn't have no teacher. Not at noon. And the element we went rehearsal two hours in the morning and two hours in the evening. Where Chip, like I tell you, Chip used to sit right side me and show me a lot of notes see. I didn't know. I ain't gonna lie. I didn't know. But I would anything he'd tell me I remembered. I don't care how long up until the day I can remember anything he told me. Told me what an eight note was, a quarter note was, and how many notes was in the bar and I remember all that see. I…
Well what are some of the different things that they taught you about tonation and fingering?
